newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein defends economy, peace with Israel.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein defends economy, peace with Israel.

text.p: King Hussein of Jordan on Tuesday defended his government's economic reform programme and its two-year-old peace treaty with Israel while calling for the cooperation of a "loyal opposition"
Addressing the first meeting of parliament since ending its summer session during violent August bread riots, the king said his government was narrowing gaps between rich and poor.
The "awesome current of peace" in the Middle East would eventually triumph over all obstacles, he added.

The Islamist-dominated opposition in parliament is opposed to Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel and sought the resignation of Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti after he doubled bread prices three months ago, sparking Jordan's worst civil unrest in seven years.

In a series of conciliatory gestures the king last week ordered an amnesty for the rioters, instructed Kabariti to lower bread prices, and personally drove from jail the most vocal critic of his peace with Israel.
But on Tuesday, opening the final parliamentary season before 1997 elections, he attacked opponents who he said had nothing to offer but criticism.

"To work from the very first day of the formation of any government for its downfall is truly a despicable and irresponsible behaviour," he said. "The government and loyal opposition form together the means towards great achievement."
He also slammed opposition parties he said were funded or inspired by foreign elements.

"The attempt by some who are misguided and blinded enough to adopt examples from those who are way behind us in achievement and development is truly pitiful," said the king who has accused an Iraqi-backed party of inciting the August bread protests.
"These are futile efforts in search of abstract roles or cheap external funding," he told the 80-seat assembly.
King Hussein said Kabariti had also ensured that Jordan's poorest would not suffer from wide-ranging IMF-backed reforms.

"My government has begun to expand the network of social security...to contain the effects of poverty, to tackle the problem of unemployment, and to narrow the gap separating the various strata of society," he said.
Kabariti's government has been the focus of widespread grumbling from Jordanians, who complain they are being hit with austerity when they were promised economic fruits from peace with Israel.
But, despite a noticeable cooling in Jordan's relations with Israel in the last two months, the king said the drive for peace was unstoppable.

"All that obstructs the awesome current of peace, whether illusionary or imaginary ambitions, is doomed to be washed away as long as the ultimate objective is a durable peace that brings about the long-awaited development," he said.

King Hussein, the lone Arab leader to play down concern at the election of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last May, called on Israel to carry out long overdue troop redeployments in the West Bank town of Hebron to revive a stalled peace accord with the Palestinians.
"The only way to overcome the current stalemate in the peace process is to implement all agreements concluded between the Palestinian National Authority and Israel," he said.
